library(tidyverse)

## Penguin data

Let's study the flipper length of Adelie penguins from the Palmer penguin data.

```{r}
penguins <- read_csv("../../data/penguins.csv")

adelie <- penguins %>% filter(species == "Adelie")
```


```{r}
ggplot(adelie, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram()
```



The sample mean flipper length is $\bar{x} = 190.1$.

```{r}
adelie_summary <- adelie %>%
  summarize(xbar = mean(flipper_length_mm),
            s = sd(flipper_length_mm),
            total = n())

adelie_summary
```

How can we use this data to learn about the true mean flipper length, $\mu$?


## T distribution

What model should we use for sample mean inference?  According to the CLT, the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal, as long as we have a reasonably large sample size.  Let's return to the `mtcars` example where we looked at a population of miles per gallon of vehicles.

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "goldenrod2", color = "black", bins = 20)
```

```{r}
new_data <- function(data, n) {
  sample_n(data, size = n, replace = TRUE)
}
```

The sample mean of 5 draws look somewhat normal, but still a bit asymmetric.

```{r}
average_mpg_5 <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  xbars = replicate(10000,
                    mean(new_data(mtcars, 5)$mpg) ) 
)

ggplot(average_mpg_5, aes(x = xbars)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "dodgerblue", color = "black")
```

The sample mean of 20 draws looks normal.

```{r}
average_mpg_20 <- tibble(
  run = 1:10000,
  xbars = replicate(10000,
                    mean(new_data(mtcars, 20)$mpg) ) 
)

ggplot(average_mpg_20, aes(x = xbars)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "dodgerblue", color = "black")
```

So, if we take a big enough sample (like $n = 20$ or so), we can use a normal model to study the sample mean. (Well.... almost.)

We use the T distribution, which is wider than the standard normal, for mean inference when $\sigma$ is unknown and must be estimated with $s$.

`pt()` finds a probability:

```{r}
pt(2, df = 8)
```

`qt()` finds a quantile:

```{r}
qt(0.975, df = 13)
```

## One-sample T test

Let's test $H_0: \mu = 192$ at the 1% level with our penguin flipper data.

```{r}
adelie_summary
```


```{r}
xbar <- adelie_summary$xbar
s <- adelie_summary$s
n <- adelie_summary$total

test_stat <- (xbar - 192) / (s / sqrt(n))
```

Our two-sided p-value is very small, so we reject the null hypothesis.

```{r}
2*pt(test_stat, df = n - 1)
```

The R command t.test gives us a matching result.

```{r}
t.test(adelie$flipper_length_mm, mu = 192,
       conf.level = 0.99)
```

What if we used a normal approximation?

```{r}
2*pnorm(test_stat)
```


## T CI

When building a T CI, critical values come from specific quantiles of the T distribution.

```{r}
qt(0.995, df = n-1)
```


Let's build a 99% T CI to go with our hypothesis test.

```{r}
se <- s / sqrt(n)
cv <- qt(0.995, df = n-1)

c(xbar - cv*se, xbar + cv*se)
```

This matches the `t.test()` output.

```{r}
t.test(adelie$flipper_length_mm, mu = 192,
       conf.level = 0.99)
```

What if we built it with a Z critical value?  The interval would be slightly narrower.

```{r}
z_cv <- qnorm(0.995)

c(xbar - z_cv*se, xbar + z_cv*se)
```


EX 12.2

The vector called `bearings` contains 15 measurements (in grams) of ball bearings manufactured at a facility.  The factory should be calibrated to a mass of $\mu = 12$ grams.

```{r}
bearings <- c(11.77, 11.83, 11.88, 12.00, 11.95, 11.96, 11.77, 11.91,
              11.80, 12.09, 12.20, 11.85, 11.86, 12.18, 11.99)
```

Complete a T hypothesis test at the 2% level for this data and build a 98% T confidence interval.  You can check your work with the `t.test()` code below.

```{r}
t.test(bearings, mu = 12, conf.level = 0.98)
```
